utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Yes, the symmetry is a bit lost here. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. A few procedural matters first. Mr. Stewart, I was informed that you'd need two minutes to address the Chamber for a procedural matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, please, Your Honour. If Your Honour can see us all the way over here. Your Honour, it was only this. I'll say it discreetly, Your Honour, and not ask to go into private session but reminding Mr. Krajisnik and everybody that we -- anonymity is required in relation to these issues. Your Honour, we just wish to inquire what the position is in relation to the transcript which, it was indicated the other day, would be on its way of a recording of interviews in relation to one of the prospective Chamber's witnesses, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I had on my list to go into private session and tell you something about. It perhaps we could do that right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, indeed, certainly, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Next issue, the Defence has asked the Bench for the reasons that the Trial Chamber had requested the photographic material on the destruction in municipalities and in this respect the Chamber refers to the -- the Defence to the Chamber's statement on the 8th of March in which the Chamber requested the parties to submit material on indictment and non-indictment municipalities. In this statement, the Trial Chamber reasons for requesting the material were explained in quite some detail so therefore it's not entirely clear what the Defence seeks at this moment. If there are any specific questions which would go beyond the explanation in quite some detail already given, then we would like to hear from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, another matter is we yesterday briefly said something or at least there was some discussion about medication, specifically in relation to the dentist's treatment Mr. Krajisnik undergoes at this moment. We have no further details in that. Mr. Krajisnik, we did understand that you approved information about medication prescribed to you was given and therefore, the Chamber is by now informed, I would say, on the regular medicaments Mr. Krajisnik receives. That is available to the Defence as well, Mr. Josse and Mr. Stewart, if you would like to receive that information about the -- I would say the medication which is prescribed to be taken in the evenings, from what I understand. Then it will be e-mailed to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since Mr. Krajisnik has given his consent, we do not know exactly what -- whether it is medication at all to -- which was put in place by the dentist. We have no further information on that yet because it's of course not directly given by the detention unit. If you want to pursue that matter, Mr. Josse, then since Mr. Krajisnik has given his consent, you are of course free to further explore that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Again, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then finally, we were informed that you, Mr. Krajisnik, would like to add something to what you said yesterday in relation to the 19th session of the Presidency, 13th of July, 1992, especially in relation to agenda item -- yes. Since -- let me just have a look. One second, please. You'd like to add something to item 2 of the minutes of the Presidency session 19th, Presidency session 13th of July 1992. Mr. Krajisnik, before I invite to you do so, I remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony, and I'll give you an opportunity to add whatever you'd like to add in this respect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only wanted to point out to the Trial Chamber, the Defence, and the Office of the Prosecutor, in fact, to corroborate my assertion that the problem of shelling was on our agenda more than once, and this is one example, the 13th of July. How the civilian authorities in the presence of General Mladic and General Gvero reacted. Let me read this. Second paragraph, AD 2: "There have been proposals to appoint observers and monitors by civilian authorities, who would, together with UNPROFOR observers, oversee the use of the artillery. At the proposal of General Mladic, it was agreed that this oversight of the use of artillery be performed exclusively by the army pursuant to an order from a commander, to be issued by the competent commander." This is a confirmation of what I said, that our military always told us that they were only acting in defence, that they never attacked, and we in the Presidency wanted to place civilian representatives, observers, who could verify that explanation, and see if in fact the other side was responsible for the beginning of all attacks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's a very free interpretation of this text, Mr. Krajisnik, but I do understand that it's your interpretation at this moment. Mr. Tieger, are you ready to continue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, I also provided a CD yesterday with a two and a half minute -- with a two and a half minute statement by MacKenzie.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I invited the parties to locate any MacKenzie statements. I now do understand that Mr. Krajisnik has provided us electronic material which I first, as usual, give to the parties to see whether they think it useful to tender it. At the same time, I think I showed some interest in finding that material yesterday. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say on the MacKenzie matter, I looked at it. There are quite a number of video files. I really need Mr. Krajisnik's help in pointing us to which one. First of all, I don't know what General MacKenzie looks like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But he now gives, at least that's the MacKenzie statement, I take it, he referred to yesterday. You have it now on the CD so you can --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm confused. I thought it was on -- may I clarify, I though it was yesterday's CD. I therefore -- that's what I understood and I looked through yesterday's CD. I'm not clear whether we have been given a new CD.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It happened when you were speaking, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I saw that Your Honour but I still don't know whether it's the same CD that's come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. It's -- this is -- from what I decipher from the Cyrillic this is MacKenzie material.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it says two and a half minutes, I think it says two minutes 25 -- no, yes, 2, 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour, I was told it was on yesterday's CD, spent ages looking on yesterday's CD and didn't find it. But it's all right, never mind, now we've got it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At the end of yesterday's proceeding, we took a look at a number of intercepts in connection with your assertion that your contact with those individuals and your awareness of what was happening in Sarajevo in that connection was on a personal basis. I'd like to look at a few other examples relatively briefly, given the time, of what was happening in Sarajevo, your awareness of it, and your involvement in it. First, I'd like to turn to tab 170.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is P64, P65, tab 128, P529, tab 49.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's an excerpt from the 50th session of the RS national assembly held on 15 and 16 April, 1995, which you chaired, Mr. Krajisnik, and if we turn to page -- first 303 to see who is speaking that's Mr. Tintor, about whom we've heard before, and in your version, Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Tintor begins at 00846040 and the portions to which I'll be directing your attention appear in the middle of the first paragraph at 6041, and the first part of the second paragraph of that page. And here, Mr. Tintor describes events at the beginning of the conflict, saying, "I went from municipality to municipality and created military formations on order from my president and this is true. Here are people who know this to be truth and have papers to prove it. We created brigade commanders down to platoon commanders. All this was done by SDS for the good of the Serbian people and all this we did as best we could." Again, here, Mr. Tintor, as you can see from the next sentence, "However the time of war came" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, 303? Where does that --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. 303 was where Mr. -- I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tintor starts speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The portion to which I was referring was in the middle of the first paragraph at 304.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And here Mr. Tintor indicates by the next sentence, "However the time of war came," so he was indicating his activities prior to the outbreak of the conflict and then in the -- at the beginning of the next paragraph, he describes what happened. "We took the territory of six municipalities, parts of six municipalities. Gentlemen, I did not have two minutes of military education but I knew very well what was to be done. I was not a soldier, then, General, I was only a man who at that moment believed that he should lead his people. Because, as a politician, having opted for politics, I have accepted to lead my people." Mr. Krajisnik, you were aware, prior to the outbreak of the conflict, and then after the beginning of the conflict, of the efforts by Mr. Tintor and other local SDS leaders to create military formations and then with those formations take the territory of various municipalities within Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't know. Those six municipalities that are referred to here were our municipalities on the outskirts of Sarajevo, so he wasn't taking them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, he'd be referring to Vogosca as well, wouldn't he, his municipality?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Part of Vogosca, part of Ilijas, part of Rajlovac, part of Ilidza, part of Hadzici, those are the municipalities he probably had in mind, the suburbs where Serbs lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you had contact with Mr. Tintor in connection with SDS and then RS matters before the war and after the outbreak of the conflict, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did meet with him a couple of times and on one occasion he even called me when he was experiencing some problems. You have some of those intercepts here. But on this particular issue, I had no contact with him whatsoever. I wasn't aware he was doing it. In fact I can explain why he said what he said at this assembly session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did he tell you what he said? Why he said what he said at the assembly session?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He didn't. But I know why he said it. I mean, I know how this assembly session went, and why his contribution sounded like this and why the entire assembly session proceeded the way it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me get this straight. Are you saying what Mr. Tintor is saying is not true and you want to explain why he said something that was not true, or are you just explaining to me why he said something that was accurate?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it's accurate. I'm only saying that I know why he was saying this, and he was at least exaggerating. I don't know whether there was any truth in this. But why he said it is a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's just break that down slightly because I don't want to dwell too long on that. You say he was exaggerating that military formations were created or not?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if he was doing that, then he wasn't doing it very successfully because there was chaos all around, armed citizens, but whether he was doing that before the war, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's move, can we, to tab 165?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, tab 165 is P529 tab 223. It's a transcript of an interview with Mr. Tintor in July or August 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, that was referred to earlier, Mr. Krajisnik. That was the interview when Mr. Tintor spoke about the mock wedding party by which he was able to smuggle in weapons. If I could ask you to turn to page 7 of the English, which would be at your page 00255238 through 39, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Mr. Djogo asks him, and then you were president of the Crisis Staff Vogosca and Mr. Tintor responds "Yes, I was the commander of the Crisis Staff that was superior to the military and civil authorities --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, let me find the passage. I can't see it. On 239 there is just Tintor speaking, no Djogo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: 238, Mr. Krajisnik, toward the bottom of the first quarter of the page?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. It's in the first half. You were president of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct. I took the job very seriously and understood what had to be done at that time because you know that the war in Sarajevo started on the 6th of April. We grappled with our guns, people received their specific tasks, and of course I went along with my people with my units there where the Serbian territory is to defend it and to establish the absolute peace and the authority on our territory. And if you'll look next at what would be the bottom of page 7 and moving down on to page 5238 and then 39 in your version, Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Tintor begins by explaining the size of the front line that he held. It wasn't only Vogosca and then he continues by explaining the length of that front line. That's on -- at the top of page 8. And then continuing in that first long paragraph on page 8 in the English and as that moves on to page 5239 of your version, Mr. Krajisnik. Mr. Tintor explains, we came to Zuc and we conquered that very important strategic point and we connected to Pofalici. However once I officially asked from Pofalici representatives to come for a discussion, they came a few times and one time I said they should come up, et cetera. After that I issued the order twice that they have to retreat so that we can make an action and go down to the city, because I was informed, I was present at meeting in Vraca where Mr. Kukanjac was supposed to be present too. I wasn't so lucky to meet him that time but I met our --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's apologies, we cannot find it in B/C/S version. Can you please indicate exactly where it is, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: 5239, beginning at the -- this portion is toward the bottom of the page and moving now it's probably at the top of 5240. Does that help? I'll start over again, I was present at a meeting in Vrace, which would be at the top of 5240.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay, where Mr. Kukanjac was supposed to be present too. I wasn't so lucky to meet him that time but I met our president, General Subotic, President Karadzic, President Krajisnik, Mico Stanisic, Momcilo Mandic. On that meeting we spoke about getting together to cut the city in two and, well, to enter the city. Using that bridge, the former Bratska i jedinstva. And Djogo says, the bridge of Serbian warriors. And then Tintor continues: The -- the bridge of Serbian warriors to connect using that bridge and go up towards Vrbanja bridge. Of course I had an order -- well, actually it was just an agreement to take the military hospital as well and to connect that way also. I was given those instructions and they told me, You go to Zuc and wait for the command, connect with Pofalici and when you receive the order, Mr. Kukanjac will give the order. Then you will go down and cut the city in two. In that way we'll establish contact with both the Serbian sides. And he continues that, And I personally believe that if we did it then, the war would stop right away, Sarajevo would be divided in two enclaves, and there would be nothing Muslims could do. They would have to agree to peace. First of all, Mr. Krajisnik, do you recall that particular event at Vraca at which Mr. Kukanjac was supposed to be present but was not and the subject of discussion was cutting the city in two in the manner described by Mr. Tintor?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that there was a meeting without Kukanjac present. However, there was a meeting attended by Kukanjac where people presented such ideas. I don't know whether Tintor was among them. Kukanjac clearly said on that occasion that this is complete rubbish and nonsense and he rejected it. As for a meeting to which Kukanjac didn't come, at which this would have been discussed, I don't recall any such thing. I remember a meeting, I don't know if it was at Vraca where the general situation in Sarajevo was discussed, and war had already begun by that time. I don't remember Tintor and I don't remember anybody telling him go there and wait for orders because he seems to be saying that such an order would have to be issued by Kukanjac, who did not attend the meeting. I think this is something that he actually made up. I don't know for what purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You were a guest on Mr. Djogo's show and you know the extent of the broadcast audience. Did you watch this particular interview, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't watch my own appearances or any -- anyone else's. I had too much work to do to watch any TV shows, even if they featured my interviews. It was seen certainly in Sarajevo and Pale, although their range wasn't very far. It lasted until the -- 1994, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's talk more generally, then, about the broader subject matter of Mr. Tintor's comments, and that is military operations by Serb -- Bosnian Serb forces within Sarajevo to take territory -- well, precisely that.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As he describes it, the Serbs in Sarajevo did not take anything that was not Serbian. He mentions Zuc. A witness told you that half of Zuc is Serbian and half is Muslim. Later on, they took all of Zuc and expelled the Serbs. In 1994 Zuc was in the hands of the Muslims, I believe, as my own Zabrdje was. It was in Muslim hands. But here he boasts about what happened in 1992. Maybe that's how it was. I don't know. No, it's not that I don't know but I don't know what made him say that, because at that point in time Zuc was in Muslim hands. That's in 1994. You saw that I said that half of Zabrdje had been taken. They went down through Smiljevici and took half of Zabrdje and Zuc, and now he's saying that he took Zuc. A lady witness told you about that, if you remember, who testified in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's look at some contemporaneous accounts of what was happening in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau would like to put a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Mr. Krajisnik, at the beginning of Mr. Tintor's intervention, if you don't mind having a look, he says, and this is what the Prosecutor read for us, [In English] "I was a commander of the Crisis Staff that was superior to the military and civil authorities at the time." [Interpretation] What do you think about this statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. What page is it on, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know about your B/C/S version, but it is the beginning of Mr. Jovan Tintor's speech at 20 hours 07.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I think the problem is that there are no times in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's -- sorry, Your Honour, I think it's not hard to find it. It's 5238, at the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You find that one third from the top of the page where it says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I didn't get any translation so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It's a section that you -- it's a passage that you have read, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Precisely the section to which I directed his attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, that. Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm going to interrupt, because what's happened is, Your Honour's comment in French was translated into B/C/S but not into English. Mr. Sladojevic has just confirmed that. So perhaps it could be translated into English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm very sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... was said, and I follow both French and English, was that Judge Hanoteau and Mr. Tieger tried to find the place and I think as a matter of fact in the second round it was translated when Mr. Tieger said, "that's the passage I directed his attention to," because that was what Judge Hanoteau asked for in the transcript two lines above that, where it says "[interpretation] [no interpretation]." The only thing they are trying to do is to locate and finally the result was that Mr. -- Judge Hanoteau was asking for a comment on the line which starts in B/C/S with [B/C/S spoken]. That's the portion, and that's exactly the same place where Mr. Tieger started reading earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My apologies if I have confused the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krajisnik, could you please answer the question, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have found it, Your Honour. He says here that military and -- the military and the civilian authorities were subordinate to the Crisis Staff. And that is completely incorrect. The Crisis Staff was a civilian body. It was an ad hoc body. The army was separate. The municipality separate. And the executive council separate. The army did not report to the Crisis Staff. He speaks here about the armed people. Maybe that's what he was referring to. Maybe that's how it was at his place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is a theoretical answer, but what Mr. Tintor says is -- in fact, what he's saying is that on the field, in some cases, maybe, the Crisis Staff was superior to the military and civil authorities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If that's how it was, then you are right. But I don't know that that's how it was, and it shouldn't have been like that. However, if it was like that, then you are right, the Crisis Staff would be at the top and everything else would be below it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you continue, I have one question to Mr. Krajisnik. Mr. Krajisnik, you said when you commented on what Mr. Tintor said he had taken as territory, is that this was also in Vogosca but only I think you said what was Serb villages or at least places -- let me just find your exact words. Yes. "He probably had in mind the suburbs where Serbs lived," and now, we heard some evidence, for example, on the village of Ahatovici, which was part of Vogosca municipality, if I remember well, which according to that evidence, was militarily taken by Serbs, and I got the impression from that testimony that it was a Muslim-inhabited village. Could you comment on the specific situation in Ahatovici in light of the evidence presented and compare it with what your testimony was that it was only suburbs where Serbs lived were taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I probably have to speak slowly. Mr. Tintor did not take any, because here we are talking about six municipalities, not settlements or villages. I said I didn't know what municipalities he was referring to, and I started enumerating, Ilijas and so on. I don't know what other municipality he could have meant. But all that is in the Serbian part of Sarajevo, to the north, whereas awe Ahatovici was an almost 100 per cent Muslim inhabited village and it's far away from Vogosca. I know for a fact that Mr. Tintor was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's look at what was said, what was asked of you, Mr. Krajisnik. Mr. Tieger asked you whether you were aware prior to the outbreak of the conflict of the efforts by Mr. Tintor and other local SDS leaders to create military formation, and then with those formations take the territory of various municipalities within Sarajevo. And he mentioned six. Then your answer was, No, I didn't know. Those six municipalities that are referred to here were our municipalities on the outskirts of Sarajevo, so he wasn't taking them. And then Mr. Tieger asked, he said, well, it would be referring to Vogosca as well, wouldn't he, his municipality? And then you said yes, part of Vogosca, part of Ilijas, part of Rajlovac, part of Hadzici, those are the -- and then it's, the transcript is not quite clear but those are the so and so, he probably had in mind, the suburbs where Serbs lived. So you're talking about parts of municipalities where Serbs lived, including Vogosca, taken by Mr. Tintor, or at least by the formations Mr. Tintor tells us about, and you said they were not really taken because they were Serb anyhow. Now I'm asking you, Ahatovici, which, as you just also said, was a mainly Muslim-inhabited village within the Vogosca municipality and nevertheless we heard evidence that this was taken by Serbs, which would, to some extent, contradict what you -- how you just interpreted Mr. Tintor's words. That is, that only Serb-inhabited portions of the municipalities mentioned, including Vogosca, were militarily taken. Could you please comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you please allow me a minute to finish and I will explain exactly what I said and what is written here. Mr. Tieger asked me whether I was aware that Mr. Tintor had formed units and taken areas. My answer was no. When he mentions six municipalities here, I said he didn't take a single municipality. When he enumerates the municipalities, I started enumerating all the municipalities that exist there in the vicinity. Ahatovici, a part of Novi Grad in the Rajlovac municipality, not in Vogosca, and it has nothing to do with Vogosca, which is why I tried to explain that I don't know what Tintor was doing. I don't know what he was doing at all. If he was boasting about having taken six municipalities, I started enumerating those he meant and those were municipalities that had Serb majority parts. I don't know about anything taken by the Serbs except half of Vogosca. He didn't take part in Ilijas or Rajlovac or anywhere, and he's talking about six municipalities here. Ahatovici is in Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I might have mistaken there, although from what I remember not very far from Vogosca. But it could well be that it's in Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Over the hill. Just over the hill. Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you said he didn't take part in Ilijas and Rajlovac. What's the basis of the knowledge for where he took part in --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I listened to others boasting about taking their municipalities, about defending them. When I was talking to the president of the municipality of Ilijas, everybody was defending his own municipality and nobody mentioned Tintor at all, which is why I think he was only in Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it was you who said in your testimony that it was -- part of Ilijas was included. But let's continue. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In connection with that, if we could turn to page 12 of the English, page 00255243 of the B/C/S of the interview.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: 5243, Mr. Krajisnik, right in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be at the very top of page 12 in the English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Here again, we see Mr. Tintor speaking and he mentions in so far as I can see, six municipalities, Vogosca, Rajlovac, my Ilidza, my Hadzici, my Novi Grad, my Novo Sarajevo. Just a coincidence, Mr. Krajisnik, or the municipalities to which you think he may have been referring at the 50th assembly session?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was here that he mentioned six municipalities, not there. It's possible. I don't know. I don't know. I don't know whether he participated. All I know is that he was in Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. Let's see if we can look at some contemporaneous accounts, Mr. Krajisnik, to see if that brings additional clarity to the situation. In that connection, I'd like to turn to tab 177. Telephone conversation between Mr. Momcilo Mandic and Brano Kvesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is P67 tab 31 and P9 -- 292, KID 31272. This conversation took place on the 5th of May 1992. And if we could turn first to page 4 of the English, the bottom third of the page, and for you, Mr. Krajisnik, that would be page 0322-0109, Mr. Kvesic beginning, so you are right there in Pale, are you? Mandic: Well, we are not. We came down to the city. Kvesic: Yes, yes. Mandic: We came down and cleaned Grbavica. Kvesic: Is that so? Mandic: There we hold Ilidza, Dobrinja, and Nedzarici, all the way to student campus and so on. Then if we can turn to page 8 of the English, and for you, Mr. Krajisnik, that's 0113, now we -- and Mr. Stojic is on the line speaking with Mr. Mandic. Please tell me I have heard they're fucking pushing, you know? Mandic: But of course. They pushed us all the way to Skenderija. Stojic: To Skenderija, laughing. Mandic: They pushed us all the way to Skenderija. Stojic: Listen, is there any way to resolve this peacefully? Mandic: What? Stojic: Well, this is Sarajevo. Mandic: Only when they give up everything from Skenderija and around there. Then we will accept and leave for them everything from the eternal flame and all the way up. Stojic: But they are left with nothing, then. Mandic: Fuck them. They didn't want to do it nicely through negotiations. Well, now they will get nothing. And on the page over, page 9 of the English, and the subsequent page for you as well, Mr. Krajisnik. Actually it would be 0115 in your version, I think. Stojic: What else is going on? Mandic: Nothing special. We ocistiti, cleansed or mopped up, Novo Sarajevo. We've taken everything. We have taken Ilidza, we have taken Dobrinja, and our cistimo, everything is ours around it. Nedzarici we have taken the student compound, Lukavica, Rajlovac is ours, Vogosca is ours, Ilijas is ours, so is a part of Hadzici. Stojic: Geez, you are dividing it up for real. Mandic: Huh? Stojic: You're dividing it up for real. You motherfuckers. Now, Mr. Krajisnik, that exchange between Mr. Mandic, Mr. Kvesic, and Mr. Stojic is a reflection of what was happening in Sarajevo at the time through the efforts of Bosnian Serb forces such as the police, the forces under the direction of Crisis Staff commanders such as Mr. Tintor, and other forces under the control of the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not correct. This is only a humorous conversation between former colleagues from the MUP. There is nothing here grounded in fact. They were just bragging. And Mr. Mandic says this here, if you recall. He said it here when he was a witness. I think he said it. I know you asked him about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I had the impression from your examination -- testimony during examination-in-chief, Mr. Krajisnik, that you weren't very aware of what was happening in Sarajevo. So what's the basis for your knowledge that Mr. Mandic was inaccurate when he described what was happening in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I listened to Mr. Mandic testifying here, and he said he was just joking around with his colleagues from Herzegovina, Croats who had left. I know that not all of Ilidza was ours, not all of Vogosca was ours, Dobrinja wasn't ours. I know that. I simply know because where the lines were set in Sarajevo, that's where they remained until the end of the war. In Ilidza that's where the demarcation line was. He was just bragging to Stojic and the others. It's the kind of humour they use and it's actually irresponsible what they were saying. And ultimately that's what he said so I can't really interpret for what purpose. Everybody liberated these areas, Tintor, Stanisic, Mandic, they all brag about it. They all brag that they are the ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's look at a few more intercepts. Next conversation between Mr. Mandic and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we -- could I ask one thing? Mr. Krajisnik, you're using the term liberated in this respect. Liberate from what exactly, at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The way the lines were set up at the beginning of the war, that's how they remained until the end of the war, in those parts, except for those enclaves such as Ahatovici that we mentioned. But the line stayed the same from the beginning to the end of the line with only minor changes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that's not an answer to my question. You used the word "liberated." I can't really interpret for what purpose, you said, everybody liberated these areas. They all brag about it. Liberate from what exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yes, yes, yes. When people boast, they say, "We liberated certain areas." They don't say, "We took up lines." Because you don't brag about standing there and defending your house but about liberating something. So one person said he liberated six municipalities, another said he liberated five. And a third said he liberated another number. And so it went on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that had got nothing to do with liberating? It was just establishing lines? Is that how I have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He's telling his colleague about how he liberated those municipalities because he is bragging, and I told you about the demarcation line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are two possibilities, either it is a liberation, and then I'd like to know from you, from whom, of what, this territory was liberated, or it was no liberation and just establishing lines, and then of course the first question doesn't need any answer. Which of the two is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It wasn't liberation. He was talking about the city. He said he took a part of the city, Skenderija, and other areas. He was boasting that he had taken other people's territories, as far as the eternal flame, which is in the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So establishing lines at that time had nothing to do with liberation. Is that then a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, yes. But he said that he had taken something that was not in Serb hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I have one other question, again related to Ahatovici. You correctly drawn my -- drew my attention to the fact that Ahatovici was in Novi Grad, at a distance of approximately 1 kilometre from one of the neighbouring, I think it is -- one kilometre approximately from Ilijas also approximately one kilometre from Ilidza and three kilometres to the closest border of Vogosca. Well, that's what the map tells me, consulting the maps, well, as the crow flies, but whether it's one kilometre or two or three, so but that's -- we heard testimony about people fleeing from Ahatovici through the woods and then later being confronted with armed forces again. Do you -- are you telling us that these activities in Ilijas and in Ilidza and in Vogosca, that that was quite different from what happened in Novi Grad, in Ahatovici, at a very short distance from those -- the borders with those neighbouring municipalities? Was it unrelated or was it one type of operation which would be cross border as far as municipalities were concerned, in that area, that is there where Ilidza, Ilijas and Novi Grad are coming close to each other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know it looks different on the map. The distance is actually much greater. As regards Ahatovici, it's a completely different problem from Vogosca, Ilijas, Rajlovac, Ilidza and so on. Because in these other areas, they took -- they stood on the lines of their ethnic he can territories whereas Ahatovici as a Muslim village was taken. That's the difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, now, if that was taken, do you consider that to be taken although it didn't belong to Serbs but nevertheless was taken by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do. Certainly. The ethnic area was a Muslim ethnic area but Serbs took it in some sort of conflict. Yes, it was part of a Serb enclave in that area but that particular village was Muslim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then you also could call it a Muslim enclave in Serb territory, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Just like Muslims took my village. But it's correct that this Muslim village was an enclave within Serb territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you consider that to be not correct because it was a Muslim village, they should have kept out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I believe that they should have found a way to leave it alone, just like Soko and Zabrdje, until the end of the war, because there were always good relations there between Serbs and Muslims. I don't know how the conflict started, what caused it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At the beginning of the conflict, Mr. Krajisnik, wasn't there a decision by the political leadership of the Bosnian Serbs to take Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I know of. This is the first I hear of it. Which political leadership? Just let me know. If you mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The Bosnian Serb political leadership.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I don't know of any such decision. In fact, I know for a fact that such a decision was not taken by the leadership in my presence. I don't know if anybody else took any such decision. In fact I know that everybody on their own initiative decided to take whatever place they lived in. Two-thirds of the territory of Vogosca remained in Muslim hands. Only one-third, the urban part, was in Serb possession.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we turn next then to the minutes of the third meeting of the Vogosca Serbian municipal assembly held on November 14th, 1992? I think that needs to be distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is P762, tab 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, and Your Honours, this was a meeting, as I mentioned, on the 14th of November. Mr. Krajisnik, you attended that meeting as the minutes reflect. And if we turn to page 3 of the English, and page RR 041149 of the B/C/S, Mr. Krajisnik, we see you speaking. And if we look at the fifth short paragraph, you tell the deputies of the Vogosca Serbian municipal assembly and the others present, "The opinion of the political leadership about Vogosca is positive. In the beginning, the opinion was take Vogosca because of its industry."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you just tell me where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Top of the page and that portion is located at the bottom of that page?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, uh-huh. Let me just find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just below the 15 days mentioned underlined, could the very bottom of that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could my learned friend invite the witness to clarify who, in fact, was speaking at this point? Bearing in mind what it says in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik is there any question that it's you speaking at this point?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just see what was said, then I'll be able to tell you whether it's me or not. Maybe your translation is different because my passage, if that's the passage, says postponed by 15 days or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Immediately below that, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, just under that, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You told -- first of all, that is you speaking, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You want me to answer? I was at that session, yes. And what's the problem here? Just tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And this portion of the minutes of that session reflect your remarks to the session. You begin by saying, "I wanted to come to this assembly with pleasure and not to be the arbitrator. There are no Muslims so one should look for an Albanian in order to prevent that Serbs quarrel with each other." And then you continue, the portion I mentioned, explaining to the delegates that the opinion of the political leadership about Vogosca is positive. In the beginning the opinion was, take Vogosca because of its industry.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know what this man wrote here but I can tell you that there was a quarrel among the leaders in Vogosca and I came to arbitrate, to help them reach an understanding, and the subject of discussion was Vogosca was sold and I said Vogosca was important to us because of its industry. And the man here says that the political leadership had ordered Vogosca to be taken, which is not true. It was just divided into two halves. I remember there was a quarrel and I said to them, clearly, Vogosca has not been sold, so I came to tell them what really happened at the negotiations, that there was a quarrel among the political leadership. The political leadership in Pale never issued such an order. They had taken Vogosca before I came from Pale. When I say took it, they actually put their demarcation line where they put it. All on their own initiative. But the discussion was, then, whether the Serb negotiating team had sold Vogosca, and I played arbitrator.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in the section sentence, Mr. Krajisnik, where you said, "You had to enter an unequal struggle against Muslims," that was because Muslim -- that was because Vogosca was a majority Muslim municipality, correct? There were thousands more Muslims in Vogosca than Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It's written here, you are fighting an unequal struggle with Muslims. The question was whether Vogosca had been sold. None of us who are representing you will give Vogosca away. If we preserve it, it's propaganda and beware of propaganda. That's what was said. I don't know what was written there. Below this, Vogosca, because of its industry, it says, you are fighting an unfair struggle with the Muslims because the question asked was: Had Vogosca been sold?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I indicated I wanted to move on to some contemporaneous accounts of what was happening in Sarajevo and I'd like to move next no a conversation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just ask one additional question? Mr. Krajisnik, only in this same portion, you are reported to have said, "There are complaints about the army. SDS organised everything and the army must cooperate with the party and authorities." Which gives a not very much an independent role to the army but, rather, seems to give a role to the party where it should assist the SDS and the authorities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. The commander of their brigade clashed with the local authorities. I know him. Mladen. He used to be a civilian before the war. So I told them, you have to cooperate. He wasn't a professional soldier. And I was telling them that they had to cooperate because the conflict occurred between the army and the civilian authorities. And I'm trying to reconcile the two sides. Finally I failed, and they went their separate ways. And I'm saying here -- I don't know, I mean, this is very bad handwriting. I said, we were slaves in Yugoslavia, we lost a great deal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not the portion I draw your attention to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I answered you. There was a conflict between the local army, the local command, and its commander, on the one hand, and authorities on the other hand, and I kept telling them, You have to cooperate. Because the SDS had civilian authority and the commander clashed with that civilian authorities. Everybody was in conflict with the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may be a minute or two early.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you're start ago new -- of course, we had late start so I would not mind if you would continue for five or ten minutes but if you say this is a better moment then we'll have a break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If it's five or ten minutes, I can move forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I had indicated -- again, if we could distribute this next item. It's a conversation between Mr. Mandic and Mr. Ninkovic, P465, it took place on 18 June 1992. And at the beginning of the conversation, we meet Radmila again, and she is connecting Mr. Mandic with Serbian television and then at page 3 of the English, and page 2498 of your version, Mr. Krajisnik, the fourth line down from the top, and, Your Honour, at approximately the middle of page 3. Mandic says: Ninkovic, we arrested, among others, a few women Turks. Ninkovic: Yes. Mandic: Who want to give. They would be willing and we will set it up here, to give a statement against Alija Izetbegovic. Ninkovic. Uh-huh. Mandic: How he's pushing them towards death, this and that, so send a team over here to KP Dom Butmir to film them, you know. And on the next page, page 4, and it's still on page 2498 for you, Mr. Krajisnik. Ninkovic: Tell me what's the situation like down there in Dobrinja since you're on the line? Mandic: We are cleaning up. Ninkovic: Well, is it successful? Mandic: What do you mean successful? Ninkovic: Is it? Mandic: What do you mean? How come? How can you ask such a question? You really -- I don't know, Ninkovic, since you became a reporter and surrounded yourself with those pussies you've lost the sense of every reality. Ninkovic: Is that so? Mandic: I swear, how can you say that, you motherfucker, and then he continues on page 5 of the English and page 2499 of the [B/C/S] The Serbs are liberating and you are not managing to film it. Ninkovic: I can hardly hear you Momo. And Mandic different repeats: The Serbs are liberating and you're hardly managing to film it. Now, Mr. Krajisnik, you were -- were you aware of actions taken by Bosnian Serb forces to liberate what they regarded as Bosnian Serb territory within Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard this intercept here for the first time and the answer to your question is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You made a point earlier of explaining that what Mr. Tintor had been talking about, and the extent of the territories taken by Bosnian Serb forces was an exaggeration. What were -- through what sources were you learning, in April, May, June, of 1992, how much territory Bosnian Serb forces were taking, what actions they had engaged in, for that purpose, and who was involved?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at Pale, when children quarrel, then they tell each other the same things that they hear from their parents. Quite simply we had information concerning Sarajevo where Serb territories were, where Muslim territories were, there was no secret so I knew what was what, but about this I heard for the first time what Mandic said when he testified. As for Ninkovic, Radmila was a secretary, but I know nothing about this conversation and Mandic did explain what it was all about. I heard his testimony here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We all heard his testimony. What he said, Mr. Krajisnik, was that the Muslims were putting people on Serbs on TV who were complaining about Serb actions so he wanted to reciprocate by putting some of the women he was holding in Kula on television to condemn Alija Izetbegovic. That's what he said, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood that he wanted to put two Muslim women on television to talk against Alija Izetbegovic. He probably meant that they would be saying that Alija Izetbegovic forced them to go to war or something like that. It's a propaganda trick. That is not a totally fair, unless it was something totally rigged, and I had heard a lot of such orchestrations throughout the war from both sides, and I heard a lot of disinformation deliberately placed, including against my family and myself. I do not support these forms of propaganda, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's not get distracted by propaganda efforts because we could talk about that for a long time. The point here is that Mr. Mandic, as he explains to Serbian TV is liberating territory, is cleaning up, has Muslims, including women in Kula, and during this period of time he's in contact with you.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. He told you here that those people were waiting outside Kula to leave for Sarajevo. He said they were not prisoners, they were just people outside Kula. That's what I understood him to be saying. They were not kept prisoner there. They were just waiting. That's what I understood him to be saying when he testified here. And he was in contact with me about attempts to liberate a colleague of mine. That's the reason why I talked to him, if you remember. My Muslim colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, before the Judges get the impression that that -- your conversations with Mr. Mandic were simply about efforts to have a colleague of yours released, maybe before the break, we can look quickly at tab --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before doing so, I might not have fully understood you, Mr. Krajisnik. Are you -- Mr. Tieger asked you about Muslims, including women in Kula, and wanted to say something on Serbian television. And then in your response you said, well, no, he told you that those people were waiting outside Kula to leave for Sarajevo. Which makes it more difficult for me to understand what Mr. Mandic meant by, we arrested, among others, few women Turks. I mean, an arrest is for me different from spontaneously gathering before a prison in order to leave. At least I make a distinction there. And therefore I might not have fully understood your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are completely right. An arrest is different from waiting outside a prison. I just reminded you how Mandic explained it, and I have no clue whether they were really arrested or they were waiting outside Kula. But he explained that a group of them were waiting outside Kula to leave for Sarajevo. I remember that passage when he explained it here. And I have no idea. Maybe they were inside, maybe they were outside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have to check whether it was exactly about the same women and the group outside but we'll do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour in fact I was going to make this very point and I was going to invite my learned friend to ponder over the break whether he accepts the assertion made by the witness in relation to his, that is the Prosecution's own witness, and whether -- because the Prosecution called Mr. Mandic and for them to impute him in this way is not proper in an adversarial system, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, I don't know the precise approaches in the system from which Mr. Josse comes, and where he was. It's very clear that I confronted Mr. Mandic on a lot much issues during the course of his testimony. I don't think that at this point, in this examination, the Prosecution is under any obligation to respond to inquiries by the Defence and I don't welcome these interventions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first try to find out what exactly the testimony of Mr. Mandic was in this respect and will whether we are talking about impeach. Before we start discussing whether it would be appropriate, yes or no. Now, Mr. Tieger, the ten minutes are over. We'll have a break until 20 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I had asked you earlier about the sources of information you had at the time to -- about what was happening in Sarajevo, what -- where actions by Serb forces were taking place, what territories were being taken, citizens were being arrested or detained and so on, and one of those sources of information, Mr. Krajisnik, was Mr. Mandic himself, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did have a conversation with Mr. Mandic, and he told me, in connection with Kula, about the event. He explains here. He was not a permanent source of information, nor was there any need for him to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You're referring to the conversation on -- I take it on June 26th, 1992, during which Mr. Mandic informed you about 400 Muslims who were detained and also informed you about the allegations by Mr. Vukovic that this was part of an ethnic cleansing campaign by Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That conversation was here, and it refers to him, if that's what was given here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There was another conversation you had with Mr. Mandic on the 25th of June, just the day before. That's found at tab 184. Perhaps we could look at that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's P292, KID 31469.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So once again, Mr. Krajisnik, we see you speaking to Mr. Mandic, as you can see, beginning on the first page --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just excuse me, it's 185 and then 165. I can't find it. Excuse me. This is not in the correct order. It's the last one. Yes. I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good. Now, Mr. Krajisnik, as we see at the beginning of the conversation, toward the bottom of the first page, after asking him what's new, and he says, Mr. President, how are things? And you say, I just said that you are a real hero, all the others are just useless. Mandic: You're right on that one and for the rest we will see. And you say: Useless, I must tell you. There are just few Serbs with such name and that reminds me of Vojvoda Momcilo, and Mandic laughs. But as the conversation moves on, on page 2 of the English, well, first, you -- before I move on, at the bottom of page 1, you say listen, Momo. And he says, Yes, tell me. And you advise him as you indicated previously that Milo Savic's brother has been arrested --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, can you give us references, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, you would now be at the top of 0955.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then you say, and now listen to this. And then there is a brief interruption when you're addressing someone in the room, calling Milos. And then Mandic says: Mr. President. You respond: Yes. He says: The first part has been ociscen. It was done today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then this was the subject that the next portion of the intercept, Your Honour, Your Honours may recall, was the subject of some courtroom translation because three alternatives were given. I didn't move to have that revised precisely but I can read the portion from the transcript, then you say, a phrase, "Je li otislo," which is -- could be translated as "has it gone," "has it been dispatched," "has it been taken care of." And then Mandic says: Yes, it's been ociscen. You say: Huh? He says: The first part has been ociscen. And you ask: Which part? And he said: That one, the one that was uncertain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The translation, Your Honour, is uncertain. I understand that word can mean either undefined or disputed. I don't know if it makes a difference there but I bring that to the Court's attention since I have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK SAYS
utterances.text: I don't know which one. Oh, oh, the one up there? Mandic: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: On the top, is it? Mandic: Yes, yes. Krajisnik: No kidding. Mandic: Yes, and the men, they've already been transferred there. Krajisnik: Is that right? Mandic: Yes, they are working. Krajisnik: Oh, good, excellent. I have to tell you, this is for your ears only. This, that I am giving you compliments just to know that the bill for the commercials is on its way to you. And then if we turn to page 3 of the English, and page 0956 of the B/C/S. Your Honours, that's located towards the bottom of the page. And what, tell me, is -- is in that part? Yesterday, when we were looking at that portion, that was not clear. Is that it? And that was you speaking, Mr. Krajisnik. And then Mr. Mandic says, Oh, yes, that part closer to me.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not getting the interpretation. Just a moment, please. I don't -- I'm not getting the interpretation. I don't know what you're reading here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think I'm now at the top of page 0957 in the B/C/S, Mr. Krajisnik. I'll read it again?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, I see it now. There is no need for you to repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. After Mr. Mandic says: Oh, yes, that part closer to me. You say: Okay, good. Mandic says: That has been done. Krajisnik: And tell me, that stronghold, has it been put together? Mandic: Yes, yes. Krajisnik: I must tell you that you will be decorated. When the circumstances are right, you'll get a medal. And Mandic says: It's the people that did it. And then you say, oh, yes, laughing, Mandic continues, these, these specialists of mine, and you say, there are not many like that. Mr. Krajisnik, we've heard before Mr. Mandic relating himself his involvement in cleaning up, detaining people, asking Serbian TV to film that liberation. This is an example here, on this date, is it not, of Mr. Mandic informing you about the success of Bosnian Serb efforts to take what they regarded as Serbian territories in Sarajevo and the consequences to the Muslims who lived in those territories?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I took the initiative for this conversation and it has to do with a particular problem, Milos Savic. Everything else was something that he spoke of his own accord and I was just guessing what he was referring to. I didn't call him for this purpose, nor was it a topic of conversation. It was just to get Mr. Milos Savic's family released. He was the secretary of the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. You may not have been calling him for that purpose, Mr. Krajisnik, but Mr. Mandic is happy to pick up on the ongoing discussions that you two were having. As you said to him at page 3 of the English, yesterday when we were looking at that portion, that was not clear. Is that it? He's keeping you abreast of what he's been informing you about throughout.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not correct. This is his incidental information about something I forgot five minutes later. I was only trying to help Mr. Milos Savic to get his family released. That was all. I could have learned from 50 others whether a part of Sarajevo had been taken or not. It's a small area. There was no need for him to inform me about that. I was just joking with him in order to arrive at the main topic of conversation. Mr. Mandic did not provide information about some kind of fighting or anything. He just mentioned this in passing, about an area that was contested, and he did it on his own initiative. People kept crossing over to the Muslim and Serb sides throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krajisnik, you certainly seem intent in this conversation on making sure that Mr. Mandic knows that his efforts are appreciated. "I must tell you that you will be decorated. When the circumstances are right, you will get a medal."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was joking. I didn't have the right to decorate anyone. It's the president of the republic who had that right. I was just joking, saying I'll send you a bill for the commercials. The whole conversation was actually full of jokes until we get to Milos Savic. He -- this man participated in releasing people when I asked him to. This whole conversation is jocular in tone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Who were the specialists of Mr. Mandic, who he wants to give credit to, not just himself?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you recall, he said he was a Deputy Minister of the Interior. He was possibly referring to the specials, the special purpose policemen from the MUP. I assume. He said that he had been appointed by Stanisic. I didn't know that, although that couldn't have been the case because he would have had to be appointed by the government, the cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I wanted to turn to one more item, Mr. Krajisnik, in connection with your efforts in Sarajevo. Can we turn to tab 179, please? This is an excerpt from the 20th session of the RS Assembly, Your Honours, held on the 14th and 15th of September 1992. And this particular portion reflects the remarks of Mr. Trifko Radic, whose name has come up previously. And if we turn to page 46 of the English and page 04226242 of the B/C/S. In the English, Your Honours, it's located -- it's the last sentence of that first long paragraph, last two sentences. And in the B/C/S, Mr. Krajisnik, it's the same, both reflected at approximately the top, well, the, at about two-thirds down on the page. And after explaining at some length events in his municipality of Ilijas and more generally areas of Sarajevo, Mr. Radic states, "The Ustasha attacks us on all fronts every day. We have no help. I went to see Mr. Krajisnik and General Mladic and if they hadn't come we would have fallen a long time ago. If Ilijas falls, so will Rajlovac, Vogosca and others." That's correct, isn't it, Mr. Krajisnik, that when Mr. Radic needed military reinforcement of some sort, needed help, he went to see you and went to see General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I visited Ilijas once, on the 28th of June. He says, if you hadn't come. Mr. Radic was a deputy. He came to see me, but this was not within my competence. I could only help him to put him in touch with somebody else, with Mladic or someone, but there was no assistance I could actually give him. I could only assist him as a deputy, but I couldn't order the movements of any military units. I only visited this place, Ilijas, once and that was on the 28th of June, 1992. Mr. Trifko Radic complained more than once saying they needed air support, they needed this and that, because they were under huge pressure, enormous pressure, from Muslim units in Central Bosnia and that's true. Very tight circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And this particular occasion, when he went to see you and General Mladic for help in a situation that would have resulted in Ilijas falling but for that assistance, when was that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He says, if you hadn't come, we would have fallen. I didn't go there. Maybe he was referring to Mladic or somebody else. I don't know who. But he was referring to both of us in the plural, as a president of the municipality, I could help him by putting him in touch with a MUP minister, with General Mladic, or someone else, although he could have done that on his own as well. But there was no other assistance whatsoever that I could give him. When he says if Rajlovac would have fallen if we hadn't helped, he was referring to my municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what kind of assistance was provided to Mr. Radic and his municipality?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what kind of assistance he received. I'm telling you what kind of assistance he could have received from me. All I could do was put him in contact with somebody else. It was Mladic who could send the army there. The Minister of Police could send the police. I could do neither.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you don't remember a situation when Mr. Radic came to see you, when Ilijas and Rajlovac and Vogosca were jeopardised?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were in jeopardy throughout the war and throughout the war he came to see me as a deputy. He came very often. I don't know what he thought but I don't remember any specific instance. He came often because he was a deputy from that area. We would sit down and discuss things, talk. He had problems with the local army, with the local soldiers. He was having problems all the time, throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krajisnik, on these many occasions when Mr. Radic came to see you about the problems he was having, what did you do? What steps did you take on behalf of Mr. Radic that caused him to come back to you repeatedly for such assistance?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I have been clear. As I say, throughout the war, he came to see me on many occasions, full stop. I didn't say that he came for assistance every time. He was a deputy. We were in frequent contact. In this particular instance, I don't know precisely what happened, but I can only assume what it was that I could have done, and now he mentioned something else at the end. I know that once he called me on the phone, he was in a panic, he was saying that they needed air support and so on and so forth, and I would say to him, "Hang on, wait a minute. Apply to the army." People when we are desperately looking for assistance, they call anyone, whether the person they are calling is the right person or the wrong person for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I am going to move on to another subject.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can put this away, can I?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. During the course of your examination-in-chief, you were asked questions about the strategic goals or strategic objectives, and on the 16th of May, you were asked about who, when and by what process were the strategic goals formulated. That questioning began at page 11, line 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Actually, I'm afraid that may reflect the time, Your Honour, rather than a particular page number but if it becomes significant we can certainly retrieve it for the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you said, repeatedly during the course of your testimony, that the strategic goals were an effort by the Bosnian Serb leaders to simply put down what you had said to Mr. Cutileiro. As you said on the 16th of May, let's put it down into some kind of exposition so that those who listen will know what we are fighting for, and then you said, when I use the word fight, I'm referring to what happened at all the previous conferences.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said. And that's what I think now, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So did I understand you correctly to suggest that the strategic objectives were not intended or understood to be implemented at any time through the use of military activity?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who drafted the strategic goals, and I participated in this, had as our aim to write a brief and succinct document so that the whole assembly would know what we were advocating at the peace negotiations because they kept complaining that they were not well-informed. That was the main goal. And the purpose at that assembly was to continue negotiations based on that platform. That was the aim of the 16th session of the assembly, and those who participated in the drawing up of the strategic goals.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, the strategic objectives, in fact, represented the goals formulated by the Bosnian Serb leadership which were intended to be achieved through efforts that would be implemented on the ground, through war, coupled with whatever diplomatic gains could be made in light of the factual situation, isn't that right? And that's what it was intended for and that's how it was understood by both the political representatives and the military.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I'm really sorry but I have to give you "no" answers all the time. I'm talking about those of us who were suggesting those strategic objectives and the purpose of those objectives was to continue negotiations and find a solution for the crisis in Bosnia-Herzegovina. To put in clear language, what we were working for, to send that out and to have negotiations continue regardless of combat activities, all the way until a peaceful solution is found. I know that because I was involved. Only through political means.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you never saw any indication, never suggested in any way to the deputies, or to the representatives of the military, that the strategic objectives would be achieved through military efforts, at least in part?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of deliberations, there was talk like that as well but I'm telling you what the objective was, and the ultimate conclusion was not to accept those strategic objectives but, instead, to demand a continuation of the negotiations. That was the goal. Nothing else. And that was achieved.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I just want to make sure we are not playing any kind of clever technical word games. I am not suggesting to you that the formulation of the strategic objectives meant that your negotiating efforts would stop. What I am suggesting to you is that you knew full well, you and the other members of the Bosnian Serb leadership, and intended, that the effort to achieve those goals would be pursued not only through whatever gains you could make in negotiation but through military efforts.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not so. And I'll tell you why. Those objectives were agreed with Mr. Cutileiro. They were our demands, to have our own constituent unit, to try to achieve contiguous territories through exchange. It was not only about an outlet to the sea and to divide Sarajevo. Those were the only objectives we worked for throughout the war. We had no other objective except to have our own constituent unit. If we had no negotiations, and if the war was going on, of course, during the war you no longer have control. But that was our political goal, even before any war started, from the 18th of March. And I gave you that map, from my sources, and there is also the Cutileiro map. There are two sources for those strategic objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me be clear. Are you saying that was a political goal that was formulated by the Bosnian Serb leadership and, when the war started, those became the objectives of the military effort? Or are you saying that the strategic objectives were entirely unlinked, unconnected, to the military effort by the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, our strategic objectives had the following basis, namely to reach them through political agreement. If war had been imposed on us, and there is no political understanding, then there is no agreement. We did not achieve those goals. We didn't achieve the Sarajevo objective, the outlet to the sea. The objective itself does not mean anything, if there is no political agreement. We wished to achieve those strategic objectives through political means. And, of course, if we had been able to achieve more through negotiations, even more favourable conditions, and if the other side agreed, we would not have refused.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, can we turn, then, to the session at which the strategic goals were enunciated to the Bosnian Serb representatives at the 16th session of the RS Assembly on May 12th, 1992? Someone will have to provide you with that binder, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krajisnik, the very beginning of that session, Dr. Karadzic speaks at length, describes the state of affairs, and then, beginning at page 13 of the English and page 7 of your version in B/C/S, Mr. Krajisnik, begins to discuss or to enunciate -- to articulate and explain the strategic goals, beginning at the second paragraph, the Serbian side in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Presidency, the government, the council for national security which we have set up have formulated the strategic priorities, that is to say the strategic goals for the Serbian people.
