The first such goal is separation from the other two national communities, separation of states, separation from those who are our enemies and who have used every opportunity, especially in this century, to attack us and would continue with such practices if we were to stay together in the same state. And then on that page, and the next page in English, and I believe it's the same in your version, he continues to list and explain to some extent all six of the strategic goals. And then you open the -- after Dr. Karadzic's remarks, you open the floor to the representatives, and Dr. Beli from Brcko speaks, and that's at page 10 to 11 of your version, Mr. Krajisnik, and page 16, Your Honours, of the English. And Dr. Beli says, I would like -- I would evenly like to make a few remarks on the priority tasks set by our president. Although I'm not going to deconstruct each delegate's remarks in detail, it's correct that Dr. Beli was not part of the negotiating team and when he refers to priority tasks, he's not referring to negotiations, is he?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He's talking about the contribution of Mr. Karadzic. He was not on the negotiating team.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: He explains that one of the physical priorities, as he understands it, is establishing communication between Semberija and the Bosnian Krajina. That's strategic goal number 2, isn't it, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And since Brcko is practically in the centre of all these events, I must inform you that the operations to establish this communication have been completed to a degree in the military aspect. He then goes on to explain that the completion of that objective, at least in so far as Brcko is concerned, remains uncompleted, and he states, about seven lines down from there, "While the cooperation has been good so far, or rather is good as the circumstances allowed, however, for definitive clearing of the area it will be necessary to have many more forces there." And then a few lines down, I would like to ask that we do not leave this place without and above all the military strategists, I see Mr. Mandic is here, without having such problem areas as Brcko that precisely defined in military terms so that we know where to turn for help. He believes, he says that Semberija and Majevica can do a lot and says in these times of war we must conduct a general mobilisation of the Serbian people so I would ask President Karadzic and President Krajisnik, because they can communicate with the Serbian people through the media, to promote this more. And I must say that the Serbian people, especially in parts like Brcko where we are 20 per cent, and as you have been saying, Mr. President, the Serbs are not a conquering people and do not get involved easily in these conquests that are currently necessary. Those remarks by Dr. Beli, and we'll turn to other remarks, are a reflection of his understanding and the understanding of everyone else present, that the strategic goals were to be implemented militarily?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He says what the current situation was, and they don't believe in negotiations. You're right. He doesn't believe in negotiations. He looks instead at what the strategic goals are. Then unaware of our talks with Croats and other things, although Karadzic mentioned it at this session, concerning the exchange of territories. If you remember, that was said at this session. But he's thinking about Brcko. He knows that until that moment he had been waging war for a month and a half, and he's priority is it resolve that. He says Serbs are not a conquering people and he doesn't believe in negotiations because he knows that negotiations had been going on for a long time, Muslims were just keeping us tied down in negotiations to gain time, and in the meantime, war began.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, Dr. Beli begins his remarks by making it completely clear he is addressing himself to the tasks set by the president just a moment before in enunciating the strategic objectives.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. He says first of all, Mr. Karadzic said clearly what the strategic priorities should be and he picks up from what Mr. Karadzic said and goes on to explain what the situation in Brcko was on this road that should have been the corridor between Semberija, Majevica and Krajina. He and he has his own view about that. Implicitly he doesn't believe in negotiations and he thinks that's his opinion, that that would have to be resolved some other way. He listened to this account of priorities and he translated it in his mind as was convenient to him. And by the way, there must be a mistake here. There must be a reference to Mladic, not Mandic, because Mladic was at that session and Mandic wasn't, although it says Mandic there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, perhaps one, you said that he thought that the matter would have to be resolved some other way. He listened to this account of priorities, and he translated it in his mind as was convenient to him. That's very vague language. Was it convenient to him to use military means also to resolve the matter, the matter that is to establish the corridor? Do you think that was on his mind or do you say no, what he says is not an expression of how to militarily support or achieve or assist in achieving what was the first priority he mentions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In his mind, he thought that that problem had to be resolved, and if I may be allowed to interpret him, he thought it could not be achieved by political means but that instead military means would be necessary. That's what he thought. Whereas political -- well, whereas what Mr. Karadzic stated were political priorities to be achieved by political means. And he's concerned only about the resolution of his own problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the question, and the basics of these question, was whether other people would have interpreted or would have looked at these strategic objectives in military rather than in political terms, and it takes us a long while but finally, I now do understand that you say although this is not what Karadzic meant, Mr. Beli, for his preoccupation with -- with the Brcko situation, and because he didn't believe in negotiations, may have given it a military, operational meaning despite that that's not what Mr. Karadzic had in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Beli interpreted it exactly as you put it. And there were others who had the same interpretation, but the basic thread was different. It was political solution. They had been at war for a month and a half, and there was no solution. There were no negotiations going on at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think as a matter of fact that you might have misunderstood that, that Mr. Tieger is -- among other things is exploring how the strategic objectives were understood by those who attended that meeting and those who listened to it. Mr. Tieger, or am I wrong in understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's then put the next question and perhaps it could come a bit quicker to an answer next time. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Beli was not the -- or Dr. Beli was certainly not the only deputy at that session or other person at that session to who understood precisely that, that the strategic goals were concrete tasks to be implemented militarily.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even Mr. Beli thought that these strategic goals should be achieved by military means. He understood Karadzic, as always, as to what the priorities were but he believed, he believed that what Karadzic was stating, he was stating probably because -- probably because Muslims rejected it, his conclusion was that negotiations would give us nothing. And that we had no choice but to go to war, and I'm saying, concerning Beli and other people, there were individuals who thought differently. But nobody was opting for war, nobody was committed to war. Karadzic didn't say that that was a war option, and Beli didn't understand Karadzic to be promoting a war option. He just thought that there would be no choice but to go to war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt but I've been sitting here puzzling about the first sentence of that answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can imagine. Could we please ask Mr. Krajisnik to repeat that? You started your answer when Mr. Tieger asked you whether Mr. Beli was not the only one who understood the strategic objectives as Dr. Beli did. You started by explaining I think again what Mr. Beli thought. Could you please repeat what you said there? Before you continued saying he understood Karadzic as -- you said -- you started by saying even Mr. Beli thought that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note, Your Honour, that there is just one word missing at the beginning of that paragraph, not. Not even.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not a single deputy, not even Mr. Beli understood Mr. Karadzic to be saying that those were war strategic priorities to be achieved by military means. Not one deputy. Not even Mr. Beli.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Nevertheless, this language suggests that he translated it immediately in military terms and not primarily in negotiating political terms: You said none of the deputies, not even Mr. Beli did not, they all understood Mr. Karadzic well that these were just political -- these were objectives to achieve -- to be achieved by political means only and not even if politics would fail to be successful, to be implemented by the use of military means. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot understand you, Your Honour. Forgive me, please. But may I just repeat my answer once again? If it's unclear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I understood your answer but I'm seeking confirmation that you said not even Dr. Beli but also none of the other deputies misunderstood the -- what Mr. Karadzic meant by the strategic objectives, that is that they should be achieved only by political means and that even if politics would fail to achieve them, that they should not be achieved also or instead by military means.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no need for that last bit. I'll put it clearly. At this stage, Karadzic said, these are our strategic goals. We are going to the conference to work politically. He didn't say anything about what happens if we don't find a political solution, whether we go to war or not, because that was not the subject of discussion. There are hundreds of indications, exchanges of territories, Cutileiro gave us this and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would tend to agree with you, Mr. Krajisnik, there would be many ways of achieving these goals. But I think Mr. Tieger is putting to you that Dr. Beli at least have chosen to speak about these strategic goals in terms that are understood by Mr. Tieger very much in a military sense rather than a political sense. And that's what he's putting to you, but I do understand that you disagree with that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Mr. Tieger said that Mr. Beli understood Karadzic to mean the war option. That's not true. Whether he thought that the political option would fail, that the military option would have to be used, is another matter. He may have thought that. But everybody understood Karadzic to mean political strategic objectives and that we are going to that conference. That's my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger, perhaps you continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: A number of areas I want to turn to but let me just address first your contention that not one of the deputies, not even Dr. Beli, understood that the strategic goals were tasks to be implemented militarily. If we could turn to the remarks of Mr. Novakovic at page 25 through 26 of the English and page 18 of the B/C/S, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Those are found at the bottom of the page, Your Honour. Now, Mr. Novakovic understand that is work has been done in the course of negotiations and refers to that, Mr. President, fellow deputies, I believe that the Serbian officers, once they hear how militant and able these Serbian deputies are, will want the entire BH, the former one, as it used to be. I think it was good that we talked today about the work done last time in Lisbon, the work that was done with the maps. Not because the Serbs like to draw maps, although it is true they do, but because our strategic goals or rather concrete tasks for all the deputies here, and all the peoples tribunes, military leaders and others on the ground should be derived from such an explanation. And then he goes on, as for the maps and so on, the area from which they come, in other words, the region of and Majevica, since what is Serbian there was liberated long ago, and the people are already gradually getting used to it. Mr. Novakovic, Mr. Krajisnik, was from Bijeljina, was he not?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that's a reference to what he calls the liberation of Bijeljina, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the Court has heard evidence about the nature of that liberation. Mr. Novakovic says, referring to -- he refers to our strategic goals or, rather, concrete tasks for the deputies, the people's tribunes and the military leaders. Now, Mr. Novakovic is another deputy who understood full well that the strategic objectives were to be implemented militarily.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he understood it differently. You see, before that, he says that the strategic goals will emerge from the Lisbon maps. You can see it for yourself, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We spoke about the Lisbon paper. That's what it says here. I thought we understood each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What are the concrete tasks that the military leaders are to engage in to achieve those strategic goals?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: To hold the lines, to hold the lines that had existed up to that point and to negotiate. That's what the army was supposed to do because the Muslims were establishing an army in order to take Serb territories. And to liberate all of Bosnia, as they said. And that is in Mladic's address to the army. That was the army's task, to negotiate so as not to lose those territories and so that people wouldn't get killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I will turn -- well, let's turn next to some remarks at the 17th session before we go back to the 16th. I want to turn to page 69 through 70 of the English, page 72 of the B/C/S, the remarks of Mr. Kupresanin. Now, this is the session immediately after the 16th session, at which the strategic goals were enunciated. And Mr. Kupresanin says, "This is the Serb Assembly here."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Your Honours you'll find that at page, excuse me if I'm not making it clear, page 70 of the English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the interpreters, it's the 15th line from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it might be that we don't have the 17th session in front of us. Okay. We found it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Begins at the very bottom of page 70, Your Honours. "This is the Serb Assembly here. It makes decisions. And when I return to Krajina I want to tell the soldiers, gentlemen, these are our ultimate goals. At the last session, in Banja Luka, we said that the northern border of the Serb Republic of BH was the right bank of the Sava River. We have come to the realisation there is a part of Brod left, Bijelo Brdo and Orasje are left. We ordered the army to realise that goal. Now, Mr. Krajisnik, it appears that Mr. Kupresanin too, one of the most powerful leaders in the Bosnian Krajina, understands full well that the strategic objectives enunciated at the 16th session were to be pursued militarily. And perhaps ultimately consolidated during the course of negotiations but meanwhile, achieve them on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But, you see, it says here that the border is on the Sava, and you know very well that that was not the case, only a corridor. There is a lot of rhetoric here. It's the first assembly after Banja Luka. Everything he says here is upside down. You cannot take this as the norm. There is Tuzla here, Bihac. They are no where to be found in the strategic goals. He was speaking in a belligerent manner. He was referring to the assembly but these things were not said at the assembly. You see here, Bihac, all sorts of things. And let me just remind you there were two conferences before that date. It was from this session that we went to the London Conference, from this session. And it was at this session that all the deputies and members of the Presidency took an oath and then it's well known who the members of the Presidency were, and it was from this conference that we went to the second conference in London on the 12th of May.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: It was from this session that we went.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, we could turn to other comments by deputies and we will turn back to the 16th session, Mr. Krajisnik, but first let me turn you to your own remarks on the 18th session. That's found, those remarks begin at the last paragraph of page 11 of the English and continue on to page 12, and for you, Mr. Krajisnik, that would be found at page 17, and let me begin shortly before the end of your remarks when you're addressing the Serb Krajina and begin concerning the Serb Krajina, I think that there is no one in this room who doesn't want us to unite with them. We are one state but at the moment there is United Nations who could stop us if we do. There is no Serb who doesn't want to live in a united and unique state. It is politically impossible now but we must achieve it. I will be very happy if we reunite with Serbia and Krajina and also to form some relations with Muslim and Croat BiH. Therefore I would like to ask you to be rational and consider the situation very seriously. We have our own plan and we shall realise it by political, military and other means, depending on the situation. Now, Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where do you find this, we have our own plan? Please. I've been reading everything you said but you -- I can't find. This you probably skipped something. If you skip those lines up there, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: On page 02149618 of your version, Mr. Krajisnik, I've been reading from the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have found it, but you skipped three lines. That's why I was unable to follow. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, well, the thrust of my question is this, Mr. Krajisnik. Just as prior -- we examined some of the assembly sessions prior to the war, when efforts were being made simultaneously to advance the de facto situation on the ground to improve the negotiating position of the Bosnian Serbs, and here too we see a reflection of the manner in which the strategic objectives were to be pursued, militarily and politically. And you're making that very clear to the deputies.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I speaking about the Serb Krajina, please read everything. They want to unite the Serb Krajina with Republika Srpska. I'm telling them we can't do this. All the Serbs want to give together but the environment is not in favour of that. United Nations would not allow it. And at the end, there is a sentence because we are in a war, there is only one sentence but there cannot be replace everything I said before. I said quite clearly we cannot do this. But we were at war so of course I had to mention war but I didn't think we had to do this by means of war. I said military but I would not be respecting the Vance Plan, the Owen plan. It's all in here. And it's not the factual situation that's important. I showed you in 1993 exactly how much territory we agreed to concede. You have a map. We had to preserve the situation and negotiate. We couldn't let go.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You had to preserve the situation? Did the -- did the situation at the time of the enunciation of the strategic objectives include the control and expected retention of all that territory in Eastern Bosnia along the Drina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. In the strategic goals, we said we are stopping right now, on our own initiative, we are stopping the war, we are asking the international community to have a conference and we will continue by political means. We didn't have any of the two corridors, either of the two corridors or Sarajevo or access to the sea or anything but we agreed to engage in negotiations with a mediation of the European Community. So what kind of strategic goals did we have? Not a single one had been achieved. And yet we agreed to that very moment to stop and to go and negotiate. You cannot finish the job by military means. You had people there who would all get killed, all of Bosnia was a battlefield. So what were we to do? Not to hold the line and have the people behind the line killed? Well, that's what happened. People were killed behind the lines, on all three sides. On the 16th, if you look at the 16th session, not a single strategic goal had been achieved and yet we agreed to engage in negotiations right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger, we'll have a break until five minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'd like to turn next to tab 212. That bundle may need to be distributed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you know that everyone is always crying for the index to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I am reminded, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It needs a number, as far as I can see, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe that's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1234, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, P1234 contains an excerpt from the 40th session of the RS national assembly held on 1 and 11 May 1994. Another session that you chaired, and if we turn to page 50 of the English, and page 02152526 of your version, Mr. Krajisnik, in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's at the very top of the page, Your Honour, in English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: These are the remarks of Mr. Mijatovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although that's not apparent from the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I can see that myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, which tab is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Tab 212, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it Mr. Josse will verify whether these are the words of Mr. Mijatovic. If we do not hear from him it will be uncontested.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe that's visible in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just have a look. Yes, at least it seems that Mr. Mirko Mijatovic is speaking on the second half of page 44 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm certainly prepared to take my learned friend's assurance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Mr. Mijatovic states, "Your excellency, presidents and respected colleagues, we determined and defined the goals of the combat at the first assembly session in Banja Luka. I think that we made most of it right at that time." Mr. Krajisnik, this is another reflection of the understanding of the strategic goals among the political leadership of Republika Srpska; isn't that correct, that they were goals of the combat?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a political struggle and there was a military struggle, but Mr. Mirko Mijatovic was the president of the legislative commission which deals with the legal ordering of the state, and he says that he has to redefine his goals. He mentions negotiations here. I've read some of this. I haven't had time to look at it all, but he's talking about negotiations and 64 per cent of the territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. As you note, it's yet another reflection of the demands of the Bosnian Serbs for 64 per cent of the territories. And I'm sure there are other portions of Mr. Mijatovic's remarks of similar interest but I was referring your attention, Mr. Krajisnik, to Mr. Mijatovic's understanding of the strategic goals as goals of combat. That's how it was understood by the deputies and other political and military representatives throughout Republika Srpska. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assembly could only enact political goals, not military goals. It is the military commander who can set military goals. So we set the political goals and he says here we have 64 per cent of the territories, negotiators and so on. There is no assembly anywhere at any time that has been able to adopt military goals or is authorised to adopt military goals.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At the top of the chain of command of most nations, and as we've seen already in Republika Srpska, was the Supreme Commander, the civilian authority, correct? And that --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Supreme Commander. That's normal. That's the president of the state, as in any state. But his competence, his military competence, as part -- is part of his office as president of the state, but that's not the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the political leadership, which has beneath it, subordinate to it, the military authorities, as well as civilian authorities, sets the political objectives of the state. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the political leadership, but the Supreme Commander. He is the one who determines military goals. The assembly, the cabinet, and I don't know who else, can set political goals, but the president of the republic is also the Supreme Commander, and that's the same in every country, as far as I know. But you can't have ten people in command of the army, only one, even if it's a collective body.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And those political goals are to be implemented by the political and military authorities of the state, sometimes only by the political authorities, sometimes only by the military authorities, and sometimes in combination.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assure you, I know, I know, I'm not guessing, I participated in the creation of the strategic goals, they are our political option at negotiations. There was no other idea behind them. We wanted to gain through negotiations regardless of the situation on the ground. Everybody did his job. I know this because I participated in it. When we discussed it, it was a platform for negotiations. Each plan we had in future was based on those strategic goals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, the Chamber is not further assisted by state theory and these kind of matters. Of course, I didn't know whether you want to further pursue the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's clear enough that there is not -- that you do not take exactly the same position as the witness does in this -- in this matter. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, what political gains, what gains in negotiation, had been made by November 1992, for example? Or December 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of this. All of this could have been achieved if we had not gone back from the initial agreement. We could have had three constituent units, exchanges of territory, part of Sarajevo, access to the sea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I understood the question to be: What had been gained, not by what you thought that could have been gained but what you gained in negotiations by November or December 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood what could have been achieved or what was achieved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was achieved was the question but correct me if I'm wrong, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Not what could have been achieved. What gains or successes had been achieved by November or December of 1992, politically or through negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: By political means?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The negotiations were on going, nothing had been finished. In 1992, there were some negotiations going on but they were not serious. We kept insisting on negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I understand that correctly, in 1992, there could have been a solution, that's the -- that's the achievement to which you referred in the first answer but it didn't happen, as you've explained, and the Bosnian Serbs kept insisting on negotiations but nothing serious had happened, nothing was happening, at least at that point or at least no successes had been realised?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, in 1992 there were several conferences. There was this conference in London or two conferences in London, one in Lisbon. And there were constant shifts. We kept discussing. There were maps, issued were raised and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, please focus on the question. Mr. Tieger is asking whether any noticeable results were obtained during these negotiations. Not on how they developed, what happened, but whether any noticeable results were achieved. If so, please mention them. If not, please tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I simply said I don't know, but there had been conferences. One can see all that. That's it. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not that I don't know. I can't recall right now. If I were to go through the documents, I might discover what had been achieved. I might find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. Let me -- let's take a look at tab 209, which is a brief video clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Seems to be no sound, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Waiting to see if that problem can be resolved, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I have no.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] The best message would be if our Serb people were to be patient in all this, if they were to pray to God for God to remove this misfortune from us, the one we are experiencing right now. This was also the announcement of our guest for this evening, president of this Bosnian Serb Assembly, Momcilo Krajisnik. Mr. Krajisnik good evening. Good evening. The Serbian delegation has given a new proposal to the Geneva conference. The basis of that proposal is the Lisbon paper but it looks as if Lord Owen is giving his opinion in advance regarding the new proposal by the Serbian delegation. How do you comment the statement, and is there any chance that the Serbian proposal be adopted at the Geneva conference? Momcilo Krajisnik: Well the intentions of the international community and the United Nations who are now mediating are clear to us, and there is no doubt that they want in fact to preserve Bosnia-Herzegovina, which they've recognised by force and against all principles. But we at the assembly session, which was held in Prijedor, gave our opinion. The Serbian people gave its opinion through the assembly that we shall not even participate in such a conference if we are to have a solution imposed on us which does not satisfy primarily the Serbian people or other people who wish to create their own national states on the territory of the former Bosnia and Herzegovina. I'm referring primarily about the Croatian national community in Bosnia and Herzegovina. That was the basis for our proposal, which puts all three national communities on an equal footing to form three states on the territory of the former Bosnia and Herzegovina and that they be connected on a volunteer parity basis with a decision-making system based on the principle of consensus. I hope that Mr. Owen is an experienced politician, as well as Mr. Vance, and I believe that they will understand reality, the reality which is that Bosnia and Herzegovina cannot be put together any more. In fact it doesn't exist. There are three separate parts, or better said, two parts, and one part that doesn't know what it wants. That is the Muslim part, in fact, one part of the territory of the former Bosnia and Herzegovina which is under Muslim authority. And they will have to understand that it is very hard to tame a people who knows what it wants. "So counting on the experience of politicians such as Mr. Owen and Mr. Vance, I believe that all this now is just a preparation for trying something that they already know, I hope, they can't accomplish."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I had intended to play that plus a different portion and perhaps I'll have an opportunity later to play that other portion. But it seems fair to say that at least at that stage of the -- of events, the political objectives of the Bosnian Serb leadership had not advanced appreciably?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was our position, that we had sent out to the conference in Lisbon. So on that basis we were sending our proposal to the conference that had given up on those positions, and I was wondering why they had given up on three constituent units and Republika Srpska. So the conference was ongoing and every side was giving its own proposals.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you had talked about the formulation of the strategic goals as purely political goals by the members of the -- by yourself and other members of the Bosnian Serb leadership. I'd like to turn to the remarks of General Mladic at the 16th session?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Just before that's done, allow me, if I may, to be extremely pedantic. Your Honour, tab 209, which is P851, I think only the transcript was exhibited as part of the Prosecution case. Not the actual video itself. I don't know whether that matters but I thought I would make that observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that is the case, I don't remember. I take it that there is no further problem with it, as far as the Defence is concerned, so that if now seen that the words written down were spoken as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Of course. There is no difficulty with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for the completeness of the records, we have to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour might recall not that long ago we asked that the record be changed from video to transcript because we were aware that the video hadn't ever actually been played during the case, during the course of Mr. Thompson's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So therefore, what -- perhaps the most -- the easiest solution is that we would make the transcript P851A and make the video, and I take it, then, Mr. Tieger, that you're going to give us the CD or the DVD on which it appears, would then get P851 and then 851A and A.1 for translation, transcript and translation. This matter having been resolved, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, if we could turn first to page 35 of the English and page 26 of your version.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the 16th session?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. And toward the beginning of his remarks, lengthy remarks, in the middle of the page at 35 --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, is it 26 in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. It's also indicated as 00847741, and it's just above the top of the page -- just above the middle portion of the page, Mr. Krajisnik. And General Mladic states, "Please let us not set before ourselves goals that will bring us down. Let us set before ourselves the goals we can achieve. Many of you have helped me. I already said this a few days ago. I keep on repeating certain things. I said this in Nevesinje before the top leadership of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and before an even more select political leadership in Belgrade." Now, Mr. Krajisnik, you were part of that top leadership of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina with whom Mr. Mladic met in connection with the formulation of these goals, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He met with Mr. Ostojic in Nevesinje. I remember that. Whereas I was in Nevesinje later with Mr. Karadzic. But I just can't find this passage. If it's on page 26, I don't see any reference to Nevesinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to count the lines but perhaps the best way is to look about 20 lines down and you'll see a reference to 29 June and then if you go about ten lines below that --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I found it, sorry. I went to Nevesinje after the assembly session and after the meeting in Graz with Mr. Koljevic and Mr. Karadzic. Mladic wasn't there. He said that he had been to visit his home village with Mr. Ostojic and he went to Nevesinje. I don't know if anyone else was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Which members of the political leadership met with General Mladic before the may 12th session and before his formal ascension to the top position in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember that I met with him. I don't remember. And I didn't speak with him about any strategy or any goals, if I did meet with him. The time line is not very clear in my head because he was commander of the 2nd Military District before his appointment, after General Kukanjac, and he remained in that position briefly, only 15 days or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Apart from Mr. Ostojic, what members of the top leadership of the Serbian Republic, or what members of an even more select group of the political leadership in Belgrade, did General Mladic meet with a few days before the May 12th session, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I don't know. I met with him at that round table with Serbian Krajina but I don't know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was it Mr. Ostojic who discussed with General Mladic the strategic goals that were enunciated on 12 May?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I know that Mr. Ostojic went by helicopter in his home village. I know that from a telephone conversation. And he mentions it here, and they went to Nevesinje but I didn't know about them going to Nevesinje but it's written somewhere that he met with Serbs and Muslims in his own village, but I don't know with whom he met in Nevesinje. When I was in Nevesinje, there was General Perisic. I remember that. So Mladic wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's turn to page 36 of the English and page 27 of your version in B/C/S, Mr. Krajisnik. And, Your Honours, that will be found at about the -- at the second paragraph in that page, about six lines down, where General Mladic states, "To achieve a goal, you need forces. I have read, mulled over for a long time, and discussed within the most select circle of comrades whom we convened the strategic goals that are of substance, which does not mean that they could not be better, richer or maybe more in keeping with our current strength and the present moment." I ask you again, Mr. Krajisnik, to think back and indicate to the Chamber who the most select circle of comrades to whom General Mladic is referring in that passage, with whom he discussed the strategic goals.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that that is the group that came together with him from Knin and was in the Main Staff. I suppose he means military men.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And General Mladic then goes on to discuss those goals. Continuing farther down the page, at about the 14th line from the bottom, "If we have taken something in this war that was not ours, we need to keep hold of it so that in political negotiations, we can get those things that were ours and that we cannot get in other -- in any other way. In other words, we need -- in other words, define the territories clearly." Mr. Krajisnik, it's clear, isn't it, that General Mladic wasn't going to have any role in the negotiating process. He understands that his role in this process with relation to the strategic goals is to do what he does as a soldier and get territories so that they can either be kept or traded for those territories which the Bosnian Serb forces were otherwise unable to obtain.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he's talking from a soldier's point of view, and, please, it's written verbatim what he says. Let me read: "If war has to be waged, it will have been imposed, despite our wishes. Nobody is asking us whether we want to wage war or not. We can present our views, declare them, do what we like. We said we didn't want to wage war back in Yugoslavia but they made us." And he says, "Whatever is not ours will have to be returned, if after 150 years." He's speaking seriously, as a soldier, saying basically, "I have to know what the objectives are, what the objectives are that I have to work for as a soldier. The territories that will have to be defended." He want to have the territory defined basically. It's impossible to say this is for Serbian territory and go on and defend it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krajisnik, that's clearly not what he's saying because he says, if we have taken something in this war. He's not talking about staying -- standing pat in the territories as you've described. He's talking about, in that passage I just read to you, "If we have taken something in this war that is not ours, we need to keep hold of it so that in political negotiations we can get those things that were ours."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, but please look at that other sentence which says the international community would never agree to recognise them as ours, if it wasn't ours. We can hold something for five or ten or 150 years. Our grandchildren would still have to go back to the places we reached and were not ours. Those who think that we can keep whatever our tank and our soldier can reach, those times are long gone. That's past perfect. He was still new when he was saying this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just look a little further at your suggestion that the strategic goals were only about remaining in place and were only political. At the very bottom of the page on -- at page 36 in the English, and on page 27 of the B/C/S, General Mladic states, "The way I see it unfortunately is more realistic and I can tell you that we have only made our first move in the war, not of our own accord. In Bosnia-Herzegovina it is only starting here and there. People and peoples are not pawns, nor are they keys in one's pocket that can be shifted from here to there. It is something easily said but difficult to achieve." Now, there, Mr. Krajisnik, General Mladic is cautioning the deputies that the task which he's been assigned will be a difficult one to achieve and not as easy as some think, right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's responding to Mr. Trifko Radic at this point. Trifko Radic said in a militant tone something like we have expelled the Muslims and he's saying people are not pawns to be easily moved. And he says somewhere towards the beginning, That would be genocide. How would we face the international community then? And then he even mentions the numbers of Muslims and Serbs in Krajina. I really didn't understand his tone to be war mongering at that time, although he did talk a lot at that time, and that was the beginning. You'll find a contribution by Trifko Radic to which this is a response.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, General Mladic says, not only that people are not pawns to be easily moved, as you said, but he said, "That's difficult to achieve." That, Mr. Krajisnik, is a reflection of General Mladic's understanding that that was part of the task ahead of him and he was asking the deputies to define the territories in such a way that he wouldn't have more to do than was reasonable to ask of him, more people to shift from here to there.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, I should like to emphasise, when you mentioned the political leadership and the government as defining territories.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Krajisnik tell us exactly what he's saying or reading?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, the interpreters have the text in front of them, and when you referred to what General Mladic said, the interpreters would like to know where you read that exactly so that they can follow you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I'm really sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's above the number 220.000, four lines up. It says the following: That's a quotation. Next, I would like to point out.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters have found it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could Mr. Krajisnik then repeat the last answer that he gave of substance? Because it was not interpreted for the reasons we now know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krajisnik, I think you started that answer by saying, Well, General Mladic says, not only that the people are not pawns. Could you please again give us that answer in full?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here is what I said. "Next" if the interpreters have found the passage. "Next I would like to emphasise, when the political leadership and the government and the assembly define territories, we need to choose clearly which path to follow, which objective to be guided by, for now and for the future. And in the past as well. It was always thus twice. Generally speaking we choose the war option and peace. What we gain and what we lose by choosing each."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik please turn to page 28 of the B/C/S and page 38 of the English. It's 14 lines down from the top, Your Honours, in English -- and it's the top of -- it's just below the beginning of the second half of the page, Mr. Krajisnik, for you. And I'll read it slowly so you can find it. General Mladic states, "And please let us not only put our minds into what we are doing but let us at also think thoroughly about it and let us be cautious about when to keep mum. No. The thing we are doing needs to be guarded as our deepest secret and what our representatives appearing in the media at political talks and negotiations are going to say, and they do need to present our goals in a way that will sound appealing to the ears of those we want to win over to our side without being detrimental to our Serbian people. Our people must know how to read between the lines." What was the deepest secret that had to be guarded, Mr. Krajisnik? It surely wasn't that you were engaged in negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if he had acted this way, he wouldn't have given orders on the telephone that Sarajevo needs to be shelled. This is a pamphlet. That was no secret. There was no secret. He was just telling deputies -- he misty identified everything. Everything that happened in assembly sessions was public. This was placed in the public domain very soon afterwards. There was no secret. Throughout the war, I cannot remember one single secret. Every last village flew what was going on in politics. Our policy were negotiations. This is his manoeuvring or I don't know what, to persuade the deputies. If he wanted secrets to be kept he should have used secure communications when he issued orders to shoot to fire at Pofalici. There was no secret. They just pretended to have some secrets.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Krajisnik, let me ask you to turn to tab 210.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is P65, I presume we need a little bit more information for you. We will try to obtain it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First looking at page 14 of the English, and page 12 at the bottom and moving on to page 13 of your version, in B/C/S, Mr. Krajisnik, it's Dr. Karadzic speaking and he says, "The strategic goals adopted by this assembly have been or will be achieved to the fullest extent, just to remind those who do not know it. This assembly reached strategic goals of Serb people which have become in a certain way our tasks, our obligations to realise them, but those were the goals we aimed at and the goals we aim at now to achieve whenever it would be possible." And then he goes on to describe again the strategic goals and, in addition, I would ask you to turn next to page 66 of the English of that session, and in your version, in B/C/S, Mr. Krajisnik, that's page 65. And this is General Mladic speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honours, it will be found at the bottom third of the page in English. It's the beginning of his remarks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just looking at the B/C/S. I don't know whether there is any page 65 for Mr. Krajisnik. My last page is 29 in B/C/S, at least the page numbering at the top of the page, but perhaps you have a different -- that's last three digits of the ERN number is 647. If you have more, then -- Mr. Krajisnik do you have --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have page 65, with the contribution by Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll just read the translation. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And General Mladic states, "First, people and the army, with the help from the rest of us according to our possibilities, have carried out most of tasks and strategic goals set to them. We have created Republika Srpska." And he continues on the next page in English, page 67, and page 66 of the B/C/S, again, at approximately the bottom one-third of the page, appearing for recognition purposes, Your Honours, after the words Lukavac 93 in parentheses at the left. It's at about the bottom third of the page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I found that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then after discussing the negotiations, he states about three sentences later, "I have to say to our delegation, which I really appreciate, together with our president, Mr. President, you have started from the most favourable starting position in Geneva. You had the military result in your hands. You and the people and the army and the forces of MUP have created it." Mr. Krajisnik, there, General Mladic is explaining in explicit and completely clear terms that the army and the people carried out the strategic goals and produced a situation on the ground which provided their negotiators with the best starting position. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not the way it is. He put it here very nicely when he said, speaking about strategic goals, "Second, politics start and end wars. War ends with a peace accord." He put that very nicely here. As for the starting position, Mladic wasn't the one who provided the starting position. He spoke as a soldier. But that was not one of the arguments of the Serbian side. What is at stake here is the Vance Owen plan whereby we lose Republika Srpska. That's what the discussion is about, not something that we were going to hold on to. He is accusing us, basically. We got Republika Srpska already but if we accept the plan we will lose it. That's his point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Politics start and end wars, General Mladic said, but in between, the army, by pursuing, implementing and achieving large portions of the strategic goals, put the negotiators in the best starting position to cement those gains. Isn't that complete lie clear, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Right, he said it. You had a good starting position but that was not a military position. Those were lines drawn during the negotiations. Completely regardless of any war we had an agreement, completely, independently of any war. All through the war, the negotiations were unsuccessful. We didn't start the negotiations with military positions. We started negotiations without any war. And it's not true that our military position was one of our assets because we had even created Republika Srpska before the war. Of course, only on paper, in terms of declaration. And we wanted to fix it through negotiations and we got it through the Lisbon agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just one housekeeping matter. That document was P64 A tab 39, P65, tab 221.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Mr. Krajisnik, before we adjourn for the day, I'd like to remind you or give again my instructions to you that you should not speak with anyone about the testimony already given or still to be given. For the Prosecution, as guidance, the Chamber expects the Prosecution to finish its cross-examination not later than next Thursday. Of course we do not know exactly what might happen on Wednesday, as far as the treatment of the dentist is concerned but that's what you should be preparing for. Then we adjourn until Monday, the 12th of June, 9.00 in the morning, in Courtroom III, and I wish everyone a good weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 12th day of June, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.07 p.m.,
